subject: [PATCH] Revert "sched/fair: Add SIS_UTIL support to select_idle_capacity()"

reviews.author: Andrea Righi
reviews.summary:
Reviewer Andrea Righi noted that the patch description does not include a clear explanation of why the revert is necessary and requested more context on the issue.

Reviewer Andrea Righi questioned the removal of SIS_UTIL budget in the asymmetric path, pointing out it's consistent with select_idle_cpu() and is an intentional tradeoff for that heuristic.

Reviewer Andrea Righi requested additional testing to compare the performance of symmetric idle-selection path with SIS_UTIL enabled and disabled, to determine if disabling SIS_UTIL produces similar improvements in other scenarios.

Reviewer Andrea Righi expressed concern that full scans in select_idle_capacity() could be costly on large systems with many CPUs in the same Last Level Cache (LLC), and requested further consideration.
reviews.raw_body:
Hi Usama,

On Fri, Nov 13, 2026 at 07:31:57AM -0800, Usama Arif wrote:

---

Isn't this consistent with select_idle_cpu(), which also skips the scan
when the SIS_UTIL budget is zero? Missing an idle CPU is an intentional
tradeoff of that heuristic. Could you clarify why we should remove the
budget specifically from the asymmetric path?

---

Have you tried forcing the symmetric idle-selection path through
select_idle_cpu(), with SIS_UTIL both enabled and disabled?

It'd be useful to see whether disabling SIS_UTIL produces the same
improvement there and whether symmetric idle selection performs better
overall on this system.

---

Yeah, this is my main concern, full scans can become quite expensive on
large systems with lots of CPUs in the same LLC.

Thanks,
-Andrea

reviews.author: Usama Arif (author)
reviews.summary:
Author acknowledged that the symmetric path may also be affected by capacity differences reported by Grace servers, suggesting it needs to be audited as well.

Author acknowledged that the SIS_UTIL scan budget cannot be changed at runtime, as it comes from firmware and is constant across all CPUs in the kernel.

The author acknowledged a significant performance difference between the original and reverted kernels, specifically citing that the affected kernel placed only 7% of wakeups on an idle CPU compared to 69% in the reference kernel.
sentiment_signals: implied need for further analysis or optimization
reviews.raw_body:
It is consistent.

Symmetric path also has this (I didnt check this before sending the patch).
The service is running on Grace servers which report capacity differences
and updating the kernel from 6.16 resulted in the problem I outlined below.

Maybe the symmetric path needs to be audited as well?

Or maybe this service should not have ever run with SIS_UTIL at all..
(The only thing is that kernel upgrade caused a serious regression)

(Should have made this patch RFC :))

---

This cant be done from a running kernel, right? My understanding is
that the cpu capacities come from firmware, so cant be changed at
runtime to be constant across all CPUs in kernel?

Changing kernel on a production service can be a bit of a process.

---

Yeah I imagine this was the reason for the initial patch.

The same workload on 6.16 kernel placed 69% of wakeups on an idle CPU,
the affected kernel with the patch that this is reverting only placed 7%.

Do you know how much CPU usage can be attributed to the scan on these
large systems if you do full scans?

reviews.author: Rik Riel
reviews.summary: Reviewer Rik Riel questioned whether the asymmetrical selection should prioritize any CPU 'close enough' to the required capacity (X) when dealing with SMT and power-driven hardware scaling, suggesting a threshold of 3/4 of X as a compromise between preventing overloading small cores and allowing tasks to run immediately.
reviews.raw_body:
Afaik, the asymmetrical selection is supposed
to solve a very specific problem: when a task
requires X amount of CPU capacity to run, we
try to avoid scheduling it on a CPU that has
only a fraction of X available.

This creates the issue that a task that appears
to "need" exactly X, because it's been running
on a CPU with full available capacity, ends up
not being scheduled at all when the available
idle core has X-3% available capacity, because
that CPU happens to spend 3% of its time handling
interrupts, or running something else.

In that situation, it will be better to run the
task on the CPU with 97% capacity right now,
than to not run the task until a CPU frees up
later.

Things like SMT and power-driven hardware
scaling complicate the matter further, because
we simply cannot see the full amount of capacity 
that is available on each CPU.

That makes me wonder if we should simply accept
any CPU that's "close enough to X" when dealing
with asymmetrical placement.

Say, anything that's above 3/4 of the capacity
of X would be considered good enough to run the task.

That still prevents us from placing a CPU intensive
task on a little core in a big.LITTLE system, or
from placing a task on a CPU that spends 80% of its
time handling interrupts, but it will allow a task
to run right now, when the capacity imbalance is small.

Does that make sense, or am I forgetting something
important?

-- 
All Rights Reversed.

reviews.author: Andrea Righi
reviews.summary:
Reviewer Andrea Righi noted that reverting the SIS_UTIL support requires a separate patch and a system reboot, as there is no existing runtime switch to control idle selection mode.

The reviewer notes that the regression points to a limitation of SIS_UTIL, suggesting that incorporating observed idle CPU availability into the budget calculation could help distinguish actual saturation from high utilization with available CPUs.

Reviewer Andrea Righi expressed concern about the potential high scan cost in select_idle_capacity() under frequent wakeups when few or no CPUs are idle, but did not provide a measured CPU-cost figure.
reviews.raw_body:
Yeah, this would require a patch and a reboot. Unfortunately there isn't
an existing runtime switch to force symmetric/asym idle selection.

---

That's a substantial difference, I agree the regression should be
addressed. Perhaps this points to a limitation of the SIS_UTIL
heuristic?

We could investigate incorporating observed idle CPU availability into
the SIS_UTIL budget calculation, rather than relying solely on aggregate
utilization. Periodic load balancing already collects idle CPU
statistics, which might help distinguish actual saturation from high
utilization with CPUs still available.

Prateek, do you have any thoughts on this? Do you see a way to improve
SIS_UTIL for this workload while keeping the symmetric and asymmetric
paths consistent?

---

I don't have a measured CPU-cost figure for this case. My concern is
the worst-case scan cost under frequent wakeups when few or no CPUs
are idle.

Thanks,
-Andrea

2026-11-13.patch_summary: This patch reverts a previous change that added SIS_UTIL support to the select_idle_capacity() function in the Linux kernel's scheduler. The reverted change caused issues when the scan budget was zero, leading to incorrect idle CPU selection and increased latency for certain workloads. The patch restores the original behavior of searching the allowed domain for an idle CPU, which can increase scan CPU cost but ensures accurate idle CPU selection. This change is intended to fix a performance regression introduced by the previous commit.

reviews.author: Vincent Guittot
reviews.summary: The reviewer pointed out a discrepancy in the selection logic of select_idle_capacity(), noting that an idle core with X-3% capacity is selected if no other idle CPU with X capacity is available, which seems counterintuitive and may lead to suboptimal scheduling decisions.
reviews.raw_body:
The task will be scheduled on this idle cpu/core of (X-3% capacity) if
no other idle CPU with X capacity is available.
The selection in select_idle_capacity is:
- Idle core with enough capacity
- Idle core with enough capacity but doesn't fullfill uclamp_min
- Idle core that doesn't fit
- Idle CPU with enough capacity
- Idle CPU with enough capacity but doesn't fullfill uclamp_min
- Idle CPU that doesn't fit

reviews.author: Vincent Guittot
reviews.summary: Reviewer Vincent Guittot noted that the current SIS_UTIL algorithm is too cautious, particularly for systems with a small number of CPUs, and suggested considering setting a shorter slice for latency-sensitive tasks to run first even on busy CPUs.
reviews.raw_body:
We want to keep same behavior for select_idle_cpu and
select_idle_capacity with both using the same SIS_UTIL algorithm.

That being said, the current algorithm is probably a bit too cautious,
particularly for systems with a small number of CPUs

And for a latency-sensitive workload, it would be good to consider
setting a shorter slice to the latency sensistive task would run 1st
even on a busy CPU

reviews.author: Andrea Righi
reviews.summary: Reviewer Andrea Righi noted that the current implementation of select_idle_capacity() returns before examining any candidates in the scan domain when the scan budget is zero, and suggested relaxing the capacity-fit rule inside the earlier checks in select_idle_sibling() to avoid reaching the zero-budget bailout.
reviews.raw_body:
Right, and when the scan budget is exhausted select_idle_capacity()
returns the best idle candidate found so far, even if it doesn't fit.

However, in the zero-budget case, we return before examining any
candidates in the scan domain. Relaxing the capacity-fit rule inside
that scan wouldn't change the outcome, because we never reach that
check.

Maybe Rik's suggestion could instead help with the earlier checks in
select_idle_sibling()? Accepting an idle target, previous or recently
used CPU whose capacity is "close enough" could avoid reaching the
zero-budget bailout.

The tradeoff is that we'd accept a potentially weaker CPU immediately,
without searching for a better one.

Thanks,
-Andrea

2026-11-14.patch_summary: This patch reverts a previous change that added SIS_UTIL support to the select_idle_capacity() function in the Linux kernel's scheduler. The reverted change caused issues when the scan budget was zero, leading to incorrect idle CPU selection and increased latency for certain workloads. The patch restores the original behavior of searching the allowed domain for an idle CPU, which can increase scan CPU cost but ensures accurate idle CPU selection. This change is intended to fix a performance regression introduced by the previous commit.

reviews.author: Chen Yu
reviews.summary: The reviewer suggested modifying the select_idle_sibling() function to give a second chance to find an idle CPU in the LLC by introducing a new asym_idle_retry() function, which would attempt to choose an idle CPU from the recently used CPU or its neighbors if the initial choice fails.

reviews.author: Chen Yu
reviews.summary:
Reviewer Chen Yu suggested scaling the minimal scan number based on LLC size and idle CPU availability to improve SIS_UTIL's budget calculation, referencing Andrea's idea of incorporating observed idle CPU availability into the budget calculation.

Reviewer noted that a short slice task may be migrated to another CPU while waiting on the runqueue, which could lead to performance issues.

reviews.author: Vincent Guittot
reviews.summary: Reviewer Vincent Guittot suggested revising the SIS_UTIL scan budget calculation to introduce a floor value, such as 4 or 3, to provide a fixed overhead when the system is overloaded, and also proposed removing util_est from system utilization calculations due to its tendency to exaggerate CPU utilization.
reviews.raw_body:
Or maybe just having a floor value of 4 or 3 which gives a fixed
overhead when util_avg says that the system is overloaded. On a 4
CPUs, if you have 3 CPUs fully busy and 1 fully idle cpu, you will try
to find a CPU. The same on 8 CPUs. On 72 CPUS, you will try even one
loop if you have 62 CPUs fully busy.

An on top of that, util_est exacerbs the effect because it sums the
max of all tasks which is always higher than CPU's utilization. (For
this one I have a patch to keep util_est for sched_util governor but
remove it when evaluating system utilization
